Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Johnny Clegg his final Journey a Carte Blanche Exclusive

Summary:
Johnny Clegg his Final Journey
Johnny Clegg, a South African icon…our most famous brand nearly forty years after he began his remarkable career is now embarking on his last world tour – The Final Journey.
In 2015 Johnny was diagnosed with cancer and underwent chemotherapy …but still continued to tour..Canada and USA namely. He’s now in remission and has decided to embark on a final set of concerts in SA and Internationally, a farewell; a thank you to his fans before his final bow.
We have been given the first television exclusivity - locally to go back stage with him on 30th June/1st July. We will take some time earlier to interview Le Zulu Blanc ( as he’s known in France)…he has filled so many roles – dancer, anthropologist, activist, songwriter and been awarded a number of titles, two of the most memorable, he was made a French Knight and most recently become a member of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire (OBE). Johnny Clegg is one SA’s greatest musical exports – spanning the apartheid days and his campaigns against apartheid, His music always offered a vision of how South Africans could find each other and the possibilities of a non-racial future …..to South Africa today, our cultural ambassador.


Further information:
We will chat to the members of his band and crew who have been with him for 35 years this is a highly emotional time for them, they will share their memories, their times.
His Juluka co founder and friend of decades Sipho Mchunu, ( Sipho was 18 and Johnny 16 when they started making music together) will make an appearance at the Final Journey and talk to us about the desperate political times in the late 60’s and 70’s when their, songs, their political lyrics, Juluka’s black and white band sharing a stage caused not only banning but arrests. Clegg was beaten up by the police on several occasions but they could not gag Clegg’s outspoken views against apartheid and the migrant system.
We will have access to video footage and photographs that have never been publically seen.
M- Net will be filming the concerts so we can hopefully mix the background raw uncut visuals with those of the performance.
To this day Johnny remains a phenomena, 5 million albums sold, he has wowed vast audiences with his concerts around the world, an insert on him at this time would capture our viewers of all ages.

Press Release:


He’s delighted fans with music for the ages and now after almost forty years of international tours; Johnny Clegg is hanging up his mic. The celebrated musician takes to the
stage for his final world tour, as he bids farewell to his illustrious career. Carte Blanche meets one of South Africa’s favourite sons.

Script:


Link
It would very hard to find someone who has not heard of Johnny Clegg, it’s been nearly 40 years since he began his remarkable career wooing audiences locally and abroad with his uniquely South African sound..

V/O
This is Johnny’s final journey, the start of his world tour.

V/O 10 sec
Johnny Clegg’s first band Juluka, was a partnership with Sipho Mchuna, but the beginning of their friendship goes back to when Johnny was at school and Sipho working a gardener.

Johnny: I was sitting with my buddy Sipho who I met in 1969/70
You were a lighty then
We were both lighties, 16 years old we went on a journey together of 15 years music was and expression of friendship and my interest in Zulu culture, our music was crossover we were trying to make a third thing of what had been separated.

Sipho Michunu

Sipho: We have a very tough time in that time because actually also when I meet him at that time I tried to invite him where I was working in West Street in Houghton and he come there my baas and my missus they chase him away and they say he’s not allowed to come, so we make a plan when he come to visit me we have to stop in the street, outside of the house and then he whistle I know the sign it was our sign…I said that is Johnny I have to walk out.

Devi: When he played for you could you believe what you were hearing from a white man…
Sipho: I was very surprised when we meet he read me in my eye and I read him the feeling was just like a magic..

V/O
The thunderous applause for the re united duo takes Johnny and Sipho back to a very different time, the early days of Juluka’s public performances.

Link:
It was the 70’s, mixed performances in public places were banned under apartheid, Juluka refused to step back and instead went under cover performing….at universities, church halls, and even in peoples lounges of some houses.

Johnny I was arrested when I was 16 at Wemmer Hostel a male only hostel at the bottom of Rissik street that used to house 3 000 migrant workers we used to dance their on Sundays and all dancers 40/50 dancers and each guy would sit in front of each other on the floor and we would clap and sing and I was right at the end and their was a raid on the hostel by SAP and they couldn’t really see me and I was small, and it was two 2 constables and one looked at me and looked again and he had a shock and he came over to me and said what are you doing here I am dancing ////…. And he said don’t worry you are safe now.
Devi He thought you were not there by choice
Johnny No he thought I had been kidnapped or whatever….No I am dancing
No safe and then they got irritated with me….so he took me to my mom because I was too young to be put into jail.
Dev: The Apartheid govt didn’t like you
Johnny No we had a lot of problems specially when Juleka started township cause then we were touring the townships/ we were moving more and more into rural areas and locations because they were not as under surveillance///
Devi This Ducking and diving?
Johnny?: Ya we had about 20 % of our shows closed down by the police.

V/O
It was producer, Hilton Rosenthal who launched Juluka, backing them with his own money.

Hilton Rosenthal
Hilton
My original dream of working and somehow or other finding something that combined the musics that I had grown up with in South Africa both white and black came together when I saw them at a show at Wits I saw Johnny and Sipho, I looked at that relationship between he and Sipho there was a magic that was happening at that point in time it was the real thing.

V/O
Despite their rising success, Johnny continued to work at Wits lecturing in Anthropology and Sipho continued to work as a gardener…it was only in 1983 after they released their fourth Album with the hit Scatterlings of Africa that everything changed.

Up Sound

Johnny: we got a top 50 hit and when that happened my producer Hilton Rosenthal said there is a road open for Juluka internationally and you’ll never get this again…
Devi: You only had so much leave.
Johnny: So I went to see my Prof, Prof I need to take a sabbatical.
Devi: What did he say?
Johnny: He said when you walk out that door we will never see you again.

Johnny: It was picked up by a British Independent record company, this Englishman man fell in love with the song and John Craig the bull dog that he is went in and drove it up charts.

John Craig
John: It was music we had never heard before you know this whole Zulu tuning, the Zulu guitar it was an unknown sound for us.

V/O 12 secs
While the band pioneered a vision of a non- racial future for South Africa, performing and playing overseas was often banned because of the cultural boycott, artists against against apartheid

John: What was most significant about it is we broke the cultural boycott in the UK back in apartheid no South African musician could play in the UK they were just banned by the musicians union…. And they came to UK to perform it was a major event not just in the pop music world but in the political world as well.

Johnny: We felt like we were caught in the middle of a struggle
which is what we were in a sense the struggle is bigger than my musical career it is a struggle of a people to get their freedom. We understood this and we met with a lot of the anti apartheid activists and we won some over.
Devi: Not all
Johnny: We had problems particulery in Holland and England, harry Belafonta intervened on my behalf in Scandinavia and the doors opened form.

Link
In 1985 Juluka split up. Sipho returned to his roots, cattle farming in Zululand. Johnny formed another band Savuka with musician and dancer Dudu Ndlovo.

V/O
But their partnership lasted only 7 years, in 1993 Dudu was killed in the political violence.

Johnny: I lost a lot of friends in the political violence between 91 and 94 , like every SA you know someone who paid the ultimate sacrifice and I think when Dudu was assassinated it took the breath out of Savuka. Dudu and I on stage we made a magic

V/O
And in memory of Dudu, Johnny wrote The Crossing.

Johnny: I never had that kind of connection with a human being on a performance we were just made for each other and he was my mentor he taught me.

V/O
Johnny’s haunting lyrics and emotionally charged sound have found their way into the soundtrack of a whole range of movies and documentaries like the Oscar winning film Rainman. And Great Heart the title song for Jock of the Bushveld.

Up Sound

V/O
And joining Johnny on stage for the first unbelievable time to sing Great Heart is Jesse his son.

Up Sound

Link
He’s a French Knight for goodness sake and has been awarded the Officer of the Order of the British Empire, an OBE and that’s just two of the many honours and accolades Johnny Clegg has received Internationally and locally.

John Craig I went to Buckingham Palace when he got his OBE///It was very int going to BP with an African. There was a guardsman on duty and Johnny wouldn’t believe he was a real person and Johnny went up to him and he didn’t blink and Johnny went up to him and said he’s not real, he’s not real

Up Sound

V/O 87??
In 1986 Johhny wrote Asimbonanga honouring Mandela and other struggle heroes.

Hilton: When John first played it to me they were rehearsing for a show and he was sitting on the stage and I said we are recording this tomorrow, every single time my hair stands up.

V/O
Ten years later at a concert in Frankfort Gernmany

Johnny: I was singing the song and the crowd went OOOOOO
Devi You thought they were doing it for you?
I thought they know my song.
Devi And they like it.
Johnny And they like it … and he was walking slowly on with Mandisa my singer but I couldn’t see because I was right in front of the stage…
Devi: You catching it now through the corner of your eye
Johnny Yes…I was flawed.

Johnny: I am a song writer and for me that is the pinnacle of my song writing and that moment to have it validated by the man I wrote it fo it was just the universe making these two things happen.

V/O
In 2015 Johnny was diagnosed with cancer he is now in remission and using this opportunity for a final set of concerts locally and internationally ..it his way of saying thank you/

Johnny:Thank you for this journey for being there and being clegg heads and making this journey worthwhile and helping me show something else that was possible.
